articles.title: Building Climate Court: Evidence-First Climate Investigations with Next.js, Optional AI, and Verifiable Reports
articles.description: How we built a local-first investigation platform—and why the most valuable improvements came from...
articles.body_html:
How we built a local-first investigation platform—and why the most valuable improvements came from testing what happens when things go wrong.

Corporate sustainability claims often sound precise:

“We reduced our carbon emissions by 40%.”

But precision in wording does not necessarily mean precision in evidence.

Reduced compared with which year? Does the figure describe absolute emissions or emissions intensity? Which operations are included? What happened to supply-chain emissions?

Climate Court was built to make those questions visible.

The application helps users organize a climate claim into assertions, inspect supporting material, identify evidence gaps, and produce a transparent report. A finalized report can then be fingerprinted and registered on a local blockchain for independent integrity verification.

The central design principle is simple:

Every finding should point to evidence—or explain what evidence is missing.

What Climate Court Actually Does

The core workflow is:

  1. Submit a climate-related claim.
  2. Add pasted source material or a text-based PDF.
  3. Extract atomic assertions and identify ambiguities.
  4. Inspect evidence classifications, passages, and provenance.
  5. Generate and finalize a versioned report.
  6. Register its snapshot hash on a local EVM.
  7. Recompute the hash and compare it with the registered record.

The application includes a dashboard, investigation workspace, printable reports, JSON exports, version history, audit explorer, and demo controls.

It runs locally without paid API keys or cloud accounts.

That independence matters. An investigation should remain usable when an optional model is unavailable, a quota is exhausted, or the local blockchain is offline.

There is also an important boundary: user-provided documents are not automatically authenticated. They remain inconclusive pending independent review. Clearly labeled synthetic fixtures demonstrate supporting and contradictory classifications without implying that the platform has independently verified real companies.

The Technology Stack

Layer Tools
Interface Next.js App Router, React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Lucide
HTTP backend Next.js server-side route handlers
Runtime validation Zod
Local persistence Schema-validated JSON with atomic replacement and backups
Optional cloud persistence Supabase PostgreSQL
Optional AI Official Gemini SDK
Report integrity Canonical serialization and SHA-256
Blockchain Solidity, Hardhat, Ethers.js
Automated testing Node’s test runner, tsx, Playwright, Chromium
Release checks GitHub Actions, secret scanning, dependency auditing

We kept the application as a monolith. The challenge did not require independently deployed services; it required clear boundaries and predictable failure behavior.

Architecture: A Small Monolith with Explicit Responsibilities

The architecture separates presentation, orchestration, business rules, persistence, and external adapters.

flowchart TD
    User[Presenter or authenticated operator]
    Gateway[Access boundary]
    UI[React workspace]
    API[Validated API routes]
    Cases[Case services]
    Engine[Deterministic assessment engine]
    Store[Repository adapter]
    Audit[Audit service and reconciliation]
    PDF[Bounded PDF child process]
    AI[Optional Gemini adapter]

    User --> Gateway --> UI --> API
    API --> Cases
    Cases --> Engine
    Cases --> Store
    Cases -.-> AI
    API --> PDF
    API --> Audit
    Audit --> Store
    Audit --> EVM[Local Solidity registry]
    Store --> Local[(Local JSON)]
    Store -.-> Cloud[(Optional Supabase)]

The main modules reflect those responsibilities:

  • lib/engine.ts handles extraction, assessment, deduplication, and snapshots.
  • lib/services.ts orchestrates case operations and audit state transitions.
  • lib/store.ts handles persistence.
  • lib/chain.ts communicates with the registry.
  • lib/ai.ts provides optional interpretation.
  • lib/readiness.ts checks required dependencies.
  • Dedicated report, presentation, and API-client modules support the interface.

This structure made it possible to improve reliability without replacing the framework or introducing a message broker.

Deterministic Assessment Before AI Interpretation

Climate Court’s core assessment does not depend on an LLM.

Deterministic extraction identifies explicit quantities, units, reporting years, and qualifiers. It preserves unresolved questions rather than supplying missing context.

For example:

“Our emissions fell 40% last year.”

The platform can extract the percentage while leaving the reporting period unresolved. It should not silently decide which year “last year” refers to.

The assessment uses these verdict labels:

SUPPORTED
PARTIALLY_SUPPORTED
CONTRADICTED
INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE
UNRESOLVED

The current demo conservatively reserves SUPPORTED for independently complete reviewed evidence rather than issuing it automatically.

Evidence coverage is separate from the verdict. It counts completed checks, including source availability, reporting periods, comparable measurements, and independent scope verification.

It is not a probability that the claim is true.

The AI adapter has a narrow role

When configured, Gemini suggests ambiguities. It does not decide the verdict, invent sources, execute tools, or submit transactions.

The adapter uses:

  • A server-side API key.
  • A configured model rather than an assumed default.
  • Runtime validation of structured JSON.
  • Output and token limits.
  • Bounded attempts within an overall time budget.
  • Deterministic fallback.

The effective mode and fallback reason are recorded with the investigation. A “configured” integration flag alone cannot establish that a model successfully ran.

Live Gemini behavior was not part of the completed local validation, so the application does not claim otherwise.

Evidence Integrity Starts Before Blockchain

One of the most instructive defects appeared in deduplication.

An early normalization step removed punctuation. That made these passages appear identical:

Emissions were 1.2 tonnes.
Emissions were 12 tonnes.

Case folding introduced another scientific problem:

Energy use was 1 MWh.
Energy use was 1 mWh.

Those units are different.

The corrected implementation deliberately uses conservative, exact text deduplication. It normalizes Unicode and whitespace while preserving case, punctuation, signs, units, and negation.

const key = hash(
  excerpt
    .normalize("NFC")
    .replace(/\s+/g, " ")
    .trim()
);

Similar passages remain separate. The application no longer claims semantic near-duplicate detection.

This was a useful architectural lesson: normalization is a domain decision. A transformation that helps ordinary text matching can destroy scientific meaning.

We also corrected synthetic source passages so their classification explanations refer to details actually present in the excerpt. A synthetic label is disclosure, not a substitute for traceability.

Persistence: Simple Storage, Explicit Constraints

For the local demonstration, we chose a JSON repository rather than introducing a database server.

That keeps setup accessible, but it requires clear limits.

The local adapter now provides:

  • Runtime schema validation.
  • Aggregate and record-count limits.
  • Atomic file replacement.
  • File synchronization before replacement.
  • A previous validated backup.
  • A process-owner writer guard.
  • Checksum-verified backup and restore commands.

Finalized snapshots are copied separately from working case data. Later evidence additions do not rewrite those snapshots.

This is application-level immutability, not write-once storage. An actor with filesystem access can still alter files; independent hash verification is what makes changes detectable.

The optional Supabase adapter uses revision-based compare-and-swap updates to reject lost-update races. That implementation still requires separate validation with a live Supabase environment.

The lesson was not that JSON is universally sufficient. It was that a small demo benefits from a storage model whose constraints are explicit and tested.

Blockchain Auditing: Two Systems, One Difficult Failure Boundary

The Solidity registry stores minimal information:

  • An opaque case identifier.
  • A report version.
  • A 32-byte snapshot digest.
  • A registration timestamp.

Documents and full reports remain off-chain.

The contract restricts registration to its operator and rejects duplicate case versions and invalid inputs.

Before registration, the application serializes a finalized snapshot using application-defined canonicalization rules and calculates SHA-256 over the UTF-8 result.

Verification retrieves the actual registry record, recreates the snapshot digest, and compares them.

A matching result establishes integrity against that record. It does not establish that the evidence is authentic or the climate claim is correct.

The failure we initially missed

The difficult sequence was:

Transaction confirms on-chain
          ↓
Saving its local metadata fails
          ↓
User retries
          ↓
Contract rejects duplicate registration

Both individual systems behaved as designed. The combined workflow did not recover.

We fixed this with persisted operation states and reconciliation:

PENDING → BROADCAST → CONFIRMED
               ↘ UNAVAILABLE
               ↘ STALE
               ↘ CONFLICT

Before sending a transaction, the application checks the existing registry record.

  • An absent record can be registered.
  • A matching record can be reconciled with its confirmed receipt.
  • A conflicting digest stops the operation.
  • Historical metadata without a corresponding current registration is reported as stale or unavailable.

This also fixed another misleading behavior: after a chain reset, cached local metadata could previously produce a success response.

The corrected system checks the chain instead of treating its cache as proof.

Reliability: Keep External Waits Outside Storage Locks

The original mutation queue included network work.

That meant a stalled blockchain confirmation could delay unrelated case updates.

The revised approach keeps storage critical sections short:

Persist operation intent
          ↓
Release storage queue
          ↓
Perform bounded external work
          ↓
Re-enter queue
          ↓
Merge result into the intended version

Investigation updates use revision checks to avoid overwriting newer edits. Audit results are merged into the specific finalized version they belong to.

We tested this by pausing local mining. Anchoring reached its deadline while another case could still be finalized.

The important distinction is that a per-request RPC timeout is not an end-to-end operation deadline. The complete operation needs its own budget.

Security: Protect the Authority Behind the API

Keeping keys off the frontend was necessary, but insufficient.

The API can invoke an authorized registry operator. Without access control, a reachable client could exercise that authority indirectly.

Climate Court now has two access modes.

Local presenter mode

The custom Node server binds to loopback and checks the actual peer, Host header, and original forwarding headers before Next.js handles the request.

It adds a random process-private gateway proof. Local API access requires that proof and fails closed without it.

Shared operator mode

Shared mode requires HTTPS configuration and securely injected operator credentials. Sessions use signed, expiring cookies with:

  • HttpOnly
  • Secure
  • SameSite=Strict

Case reads, reports, mutations, reset controls, and blockchain actions require authorization.

Additional protections include server-only credential modules, sanitized API errors, secret scanning, staged-content checks, request budgets, and browser security headers.

PDF extraction runs in a separate process with a bounded heap, page/text limits, a deadline, and no inherited application credentials. This provides resource isolation; it is not an OS security sandbox.

Readiness, Observability, and Recovery

A health endpoint that always says “ok” is not a readiness check.

We separated:

  • Liveness: the process can answer.
  • Readiness: required configuration, storage, and dependencies are usable.

The demo preflight also performs a functional case read and checks the local registry and operator.

Operational events contain an operation name, request ID, outcome, allowlisted diagnostic code, and duration. Raw SDK errors, credentials, request bodies, and source documents are excluded.

Recovery is documented and executable. Backup restoration validates the manifest, stored structure, and finalized snapshot digests, while preserving replaced data for inspection.

Local report backups do not restore ephemeral blockchain history. The runbook makes that distinction explicit.

How Architectural Best Practices Helped

We used established frameworks as review lenses rather than claiming formal certification.

Principle Concrete application
AWS Well-Architected reliability Bounded operations, dependency readiness, reconciliation, tested restoration
OWASP access control Authorization around report data and operator-backed actions
OWASP secrets and error handling Server-only modules, secret checks, sanitized public errors
12-Factor configuration Runtime configuration and optional backing-service adapters
SOLID separation of concerns Independent services, repository boundary, extracted presentation modules
Google SRE principles Failure injection, truthful status, operational budgets, recovery rehearsals
ISO/IEC 25010 Correctness, recoverability, maintainability, and measured resource behavior
NIST SSDF Repeatable CI gates, dependency review, security regression tests
AI risk management Narrow model authority, explicit uncertainty, provenance, bounded fallback

The most useful outcome was a prioritized list of small changes. None required an enterprise-scale rewrite.

What Went Well

The final local validation included:

  • 34 passing automated tests.
  • HTTP and desktop/mobile browser workflows.
  • Browser upload, retry, and refresh failure paths.
  • Real transaction confirmation followed by local persistence failure.
  • Chain stalls, resets, and conflicting digests.
  • Backup, restore, restart, and operator-access checks.
  • Ten consecutive complete claim-to-verification rehearsals.

A bounded local resource rehearsal used 20 load cases, five 1,000-word sources per case, and three snapshots each.

After warm-up, across 20 measured iterations:

Measurement Observed
Read latency p95 24 ms
Write latency p95 54 ms
Peak RSS 288 MiB

These are local observations, not hosted availability guarantees.

The production dependency audit reported zero vulnerabilities after patching Zod and PostCSS. A separate full-tree audit still identified development-tool advisories; their applicability and residual risks are documented rather than hidden.

What We Learned

The happy path is weak evidence of reliability. The most valuable tests interrupted the workflow between successful steps.

Retries are part of the architecture. An error message cannot compensate for an operation that is unsafe to repeat.

Truthful status is a correctness requirement. “Configured,” “registered,” “confirmed,” and “verified” describe different facts.

Scientific text needs conservative processing. Decimal points, signs, scope, units, and casing can change the meaning of evidence.

AI availability should not determine application availability. A narrow optional adapter made fallback straightforward.

A monolith can have strong boundaries. Separating responsibilities and shortening critical sections solved the demonstrated problems without multiplying infrastructure.

What Comes Next

The next useful capability is a human-reviewed evidence classification workflow, with stronger provenance and richer comparisons across reporting periods and emissions scopes.

Other planned work includes live validation of the optional Gemini and Supabase adapters, authenticated collaboration, and public-testnet integration.

Those are separate deployment and product scopes. The current evidence supports a controlled local single-operator demonstration—not a claim of public production readiness.

Climate Court’s goal remains consistent: help users follow the evidence, preserve uncertainty, and make the resulting investigation independently inspectable.

articles.title: AbortSignal.timeout() and AbortSignal.any(): Cancel Any Async Call in TypeScript
articles.description: Your setTimeout timeout gives up on the request but never stops it. AbortSignal.timeout(), any() and throwIfAborted() fix that, with no casts.
articles.body_html:
• Book: TypeScript Essentials
  • Also by me: The TypeScript Library — the 5-book collection
  • My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools
  • Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub

Your function promised to give up after two seconds, and it did. It threw a nice Error("timed out"), the caller logged it, the user saw a retry button. Meanwhile the HTTP request it was supposed to abandon kept downloading for another forty seconds, holding a socket, filling a buffer nobody would ever read.

That is what a hand-rolled timeout built on setTimeout and Promise.race does. It stops waiting. It never stops the work.

The fix has been sitting in every runtime for a while. Node.js added AbortSignal.timeout() in v17.3.0 and v16.14.0, and AbortSignal.any() in v20.3.0 and v18.17.0. MDN marks AbortSignal.any() as available across browsers since March 2024, and AbortSignal.timeout() since April 2024. Deno and Bun document both too.

Every snippet below is plain TypeScript that runs with node file.ts. Node's type stripping is on by default from v23.6.0 and v22.18.0, and stable since v25.2.0 and v24.12.0. On an older Node, use tsx. The snippets use top-level await, so run them in a folder whose package.json has "type": "module".

The setTimeout-and-a-flag version, and what it leaks

Here is the pattern you will find in a lot of codebases:

// race.ts: the hand-rolled timeout
async function getJson(url: string, ms: number) {
  let timedOut = false;
  const timer = new Promise<never>((_, reject) => {
    setTimeout(() => {
      timedOut = true;
      reject(new Error(`timed out after ${ms}ms`));
    }, ms);
  });
  const work = fetch(url).then((res) => {
    if (timedOut) return undefined; // too late, drop it
    return res.json();
  });
  return Promise.race([work, timer]);
}

Read it as the runtime does. Promise.race settles with whichever promise finishes first, and that is all it does. It has no way to reach into the fetch and stop it. The timedOut flag only protects your code from using a late result. The connection, the response stream and the JSON parse you skipped are still the runtime's problem.

There is a second leak in the happy path. When work wins, the timer is never cleared, so the pending setTimeout keeps the process alive until it fires, long after the response is in. A CLI built this way sits there doing nothing until the timer runs out.

Bun's own linter has a rule for the controller-plus-timer variant of this, prefer-timeout-signal, which flags an AbortController that only a setTimeout aborts.

AbortSignal.timeout(): one call, one deadline

fetch takes a signal option. Hand it a signal that aborts itself after a delay and the runtime tears down the request when the deadline hits:

// timeout.ts
try {
  const res = await fetch("https://example.com/", {
    signal: AbortSignal.timeout(2_000),
  });
  const body = await res.text();
  console.log(res.status, body.length);
} catch (err) {
  console.error("request failed:", err);
}

There is no timer to clear and no flag to check. Node's docs describe it as returning "a new AbortSignal which will be aborted in delay milliseconds" (globals docs).

The reason it aborts with matters for later. Per MDN, the signal's reason is a DOMException named TimeoutError. Deno's fetch timeout example spells out what that means for fetch: "When the deadline passes first, fetch rejects with a DOMException whose name is TimeoutError, not AbortError." A plain controller.abort() with no argument, by contrast, uses an AbortError DOMException as the reason (MDN).

Keep res.text() inside the try. The body arrives after the headers, and a slow body is exactly the case a deadline exists for.

One trap: the clock starts when you call AbortSignal.timeout(), not when you pass the signal to something. Create it per call. A module-level const DEADLINE = AbortSignal.timeout(5_000) is already aborted for every request made after the first five seconds of the process.

AbortSignal.any(): a user cancel and a deadline on one signal

Real calls rarely have one reason to stop. The user hits cancel, the server is shutting down, or the deadline passes. AbortSignal.any() takes a list of signals and returns one that aborts when any of them does. Per MDN, its reason is the reason of the first input that aborted.

// any.ts
const user = new AbortController();
process.once("SIGINT", () => user.abort());

const signal = AbortSignal.any([
  user.signal,
  AbortSignal.timeout(10_000),
]);

try {
  const res = await fetch("https://example.com/", { signal });
  console.log(res.status, (await res.text()).length);
} catch (err) {
  console.error("stopped:", signal.reason);
}

Press Ctrl-C during the request and the combined signal aborts with the AbortError from user.abort(). If the request is still running at ten seconds, it aborts with the TimeoutError.

This composes well with retries. Each attempt gets its own short deadline, and all of them share the user's cancel and one overall budget:

// retry.ts
async function getWithRetry(
  url: string,
  outer: AbortSignal,
): Promise<Response> {
  const budget = AbortSignal.timeout(8_000);
  for (let attempt = 1; ; attempt++) {
    const signal = AbortSignal.any([
      outer,
      budget,
      AbortSignal.timeout(2_000),
    ]);
    try {
      return await fetch(url, { signal });
    } catch (err) {
      // the caller or the budget gave up: stop retrying
      if (outer.aborted || budget.aborted) throw err;
      if (attempt === 3) throw err;
    }
  }
}

const user = new AbortController();
const res = await getWithRetry(
  "https://example.com/",
  user.signal,
);
console.log(res.status);

The returned body is still bound to those deadlines. If it can be slow, read it inside getWithRetry, or the 2-second attempt timer can fire mid-download.

Notice the check inside catch. It asks the signals what happened instead of guessing from the error.

Make your own async functions cancellable

Passing signal to fetch covers the network. Your own loops, polls and multi-step jobs need to cooperate too, and signal.throwIfAborted() is the one-liner for that. It throws the signal's reason if the signal has aborted and does nothing otherwise (MDN).

The pattern: accept a signal, check it before each unit of work, and pass it down to everything that accepts one.

// poll.ts
import { setTimeout as sleep } from "node:timers/promises";

type Job = { id: string; done: boolean };

export async function waitForJob(
  check: (signal: AbortSignal) => Promise<Job>,
  signal: AbortSignal,
): Promise<Job> {
  while (true) {
    signal.throwIfAborted();
    const job = await check(signal);
    if (job.done) return job;
    await sleep(500, undefined, { signal });
  }
}

let calls = 0;
const check = async (): Promise<Job> => {
  calls += 1;
  return { id: "job-1", done: calls > 100 };
};

const deadline = AbortSignal.timeout(1_200);
try {
  await waitForJob(check, deadline);
} catch (err) {
  console.error("gave up:", deadline.reason);
}

Three places can stop this loop: the throwIfAborted() at the top of each iteration, the check function if it forwards the signal to a fetch, and the sleep. timers/promises accepts a signal and, when it is cancelled, rejects with an 'AbortError'.

The deadline above fires while the loop is sleeping, so the error that reaches your catch comes from the sleep. Node's errors docs say Node APIs throw "a Node.js AbortError", a regular Error with name 'AbortError' and code 'ABORT_ERR'. Its name says cancelled even though the cause was a timeout. The reliable place to look is deadline.reason.

Narrow the error without a cast

With strict on, the variable in a catch clause is unknown (useUnknownInCatchVariables, TypeScript 4.4), and err.name does not compile. The usual escape hatch is (err as DOMException).name, which compiles and lies whenever the thing thrown was a Node AbortError, a TypeError from a refused connection, or the string you passed to controller.abort("shutdown"). The reason can be any JavaScript value.

TypeScript 4.9 made in narrowing work on types that do not list the property, which is all you need to read a name safely:

// abort-kind.ts
export type AbortKind = "timeout" | "cancelled" | "other";

export function errorName(err: unknown): string | undefined {
  if (
    typeof err === "object" &&
    err !== null &&
    "name" in err &&
    typeof err.name === "string"
  ) {
    return err.name;
  }
  return undefined;
}

export function abortKind(
  err: unknown,
  signal: AbortSignal,
): AbortKind {
  if (signal.aborted) {
    const why = errorName(signal.reason);
    return why === "TimeoutError" ? "timeout" : "cancelled";
  }
  const name = errorName(err);
  if (name === "TimeoutError") return "timeout";
  if (name === "AbortError") return "cancelled";
  return "other";
}

abortKind checks the signal first. If the signal you own has aborted, its reason is the truth, whatever the error looks like by the time it bubbles up through a library or a Node timer. Only when the signal is still live does it fall back to the error's name, which covers a dependency that aborted on its own. Anything else is a real failure: a network error, a 500 you turned into an exception, a bug.

In practice the call site reads like this:

// use-kind.ts
import { abortKind } from "./abort-kind.ts";

const user = new AbortController();
const signal = AbortSignal.any([
  user.signal,
  AbortSignal.timeout(2_000),
]);

try {
  const res = await fetch("https://example.com/", { signal });
  console.log(res.status);
} catch (err) {
  const kind = abortKind(err, signal);
  if (kind === "other") throw err;
  console.log(`request ${kind}`);
}

The .ts extension in the import is required when Node strips types itself (Node docs).

No casts. If someone later throws a custom error class or aborts with a plain string, the code still type-checks and still lands in a sensible branch.

Where this goes wrong

A few edges worth knowing before you roll it out.

The timeout counts active time. MDN notes the timer is effectively paused in a suspended worker or while a page sits in the back-forward cache (MDN). For a browser tab that comes back from bfcache, "two seconds" means two seconds of running.

A combined signal cannot be detached. MDN says there is no way to unsubscribe the result of AbortSignal.any() from its inputs, and that a non-aborted combined signal with abort listeners stays alive while its sources do. If you add a listener, remove it when the work finishes:

// listen.ts
export function onAbort(
  signal: AbortSignal,
  fn: () => void,
): () => void {
  signal.addEventListener("abort", fn, { once: true });
  return () => signal.removeEventListener("abort", fn);
}

Call the returned function in a finally. That matters most for a long-lived signal, such as one tied to server shutdown, that thousands of requests combine with.

Code that ignores the signal keeps running. A synchronous CPU loop, a library without a signal option, or a function that forgets to pass it down will finish its work no matter what. Thread the signal through every layer you own and put throwIfAborted() between steps that do not take one.

Type checking. node file.ts strips types without checking them. When you run tsc, the declarations come from @types/node, which declares any(), timeout() and throwIfAborted(), or from the dom lib in a browser project. Set allowImportingTsExtensions (with noEmit) or rewriteRelativeImportExtensions so tsc accepts the .ts imports.

If this was useful

Most of this post is two things TypeScript Essentials spends real time on: async code that cleans up after itself, and narrowing an unknown into something you can trust without reaching for as. If the abortKind helper was the useful part, that book is the place to go next. If you already live in generics and want the type-level side, The TypeScript Type System picks up where it stops.

  • TypeScript Essentials — types, narrowing, modules, async, daily-driver tooling
  • The TypeScript Type System — generics, mapped/conditional types, infer, template literals, branded types
  • Kotlin and Java to TypeScript — JVM developers moving to TypeScript
  • PHP to TypeScript — PHP 8+ developers moving to TypeScript
  • TypeScript in Production — tsconfig, build tools, monorepos, library authoring, dual ESM/CJS, JSR

Books 1 and 2 are the core path. Coming from Kotlin or Java, or from PHP 8+, swap in book 3 or 4 for the first one. Book 5 is for anyone shipping TypeScript at work.

I also build Hermes IDE (GitHub), an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools, so weigh this mention with that in mind.

All five books ship in ebook, paperback, and hardcover.

articles.title: My AI Coding Workflow, v3
articles.description: My AI coding workflow changes every few months, so I give it version numbers. New tools ship, models...
articles.body_html:
My AI coding workflow changes every few months, so I give it version numbers. New tools ship, models get better, and steps that needed hand-holding last spring now run on their own.

v1 was plan mode and a hand-written SPEC.md. v2 turned that into TracerKit. This post is v3: every step now lives in helderberto/agent-skills.

The idea of v3 fits in one line: each step that used to be a prompt is now a skill, and each "please remember to" is now a check that fails.

Why I moved off TracerKit (v2)

TracerKit worked, but it was a separate tool with its own release cycle. Every tweak to a step meant a change there, a release, and an update in each project. I wanted a simpler way to ship updates and add new skills.

I was already keeping my other skills in agent-skills. Moving the spec flow next to them put everything in one place. Now changing a step or adding a skill is one commit.

The ideas from TracerKit survived: interviews before specs, tracer-bullet tickets, verification before a task counts as done. They live in the same repo as the rest of my skills.

Standing on two repos

I didn't design v3 from scratch. Most of it comes from two repos, and I took what I think is the best of each.

From Matt Pocock's skills I took the shape of the flow:

  • grill-me, the interview that runs until a plan has no open branches
  • to-spec and to-tickets, with tracer-bullet tickets and blocking links
  • diagnosing-bugs, the phased debugging loop
  • tdd, prototype, domain-modeling, codebase-design and retro

From Addy Osmani's agent-skills I took the engineering depth inside each step:

  • frontend-ui-engineering, for decisions to make before writing a component
  • source-driven-development, so code follows the docs for the installed version
  • security-and-hardening and performance-optimization

Then I cut each one down to what changes the agent's behavior in my projects, and gave them one namespace: /hb:.

The flow at a glance

A feature moves through eight commands:

flowchart LR
  accTitle: The v3 flow
  accDescr: Plan with triage, grill, to-spec and to-tickets. Build with build and review. Ship with to-pr and retro. Small fixes skip from triage straight to build.
  subgraph Plan
    direction TB
    triage --> grill --> spec[to-spec] --> tickets[to-tickets]
  end
  subgraph Build
    direction TB
    build --> review
  end
  subgraph Ship
    direction TB
    pr[to-pr] --> retro
  end
  Plan --> Build --> Ship

Not every task needs all of them. /hb:triage sizes the work and names where to start. A small fix goes straight to /hb:build.

Skills replace prompts

I no longer write the prompts from v1. I wrote them once, as skills, and now I refine the skills. I made the case for this in Skills Are the New CLI.

Take the same dark mode toggle. In v1, I opened plan mode and wrote a paragraph asking Claude to discuss the approach and generate a spec. Now it starts with one command:

/hb:grill dark mode

The grill interviews me in rounds. Each round asks every question I can answer right now, each with a recommended answer, so a bare "yes" accepts it. Settled terms go to a glossary, and hard-to-reverse decisions become ADRs as they land.

Then the conversation becomes artifacts:

/hb:to-spec dark-mode
/hb:to-tickets dark-mode

The spec lands in .specs/specs/dark-mode.md. The tickets are thin vertical slices with blocking edges, so the agent knows which one is unblocked next. The v1 checklist is still there, but now it has an order.

Building is one command too:

/hb:build dark-mode

It takes the next unblocked ticket, works test-first, runs the project's checks and commits. With --all, it fans tickets out to parallel subagents after one approval.

Two commands close it out. /hb:review sends the diff to several reviewers and merges their findings into one ranked verdict. /hb:to-pr runs the checks, pushes, opens the PR and watches CI.

Guardrails over instructions

Instructions in a prompt get skipped under pressure. A check that fails does not. So most of my guardrails are things that exit with an error:

  • /hb:check runs the project's own lint, types and tests before every commit
  • Coverage limits fail the build, so "add tests" is never a request
  • hitl tickets stop /hb:build --all before work that needs a human
  • /hb:safe-repo --diff scans the branch for secrets before a PR goes up
  • harden lists changes that need my approval first: auth, PII, CORS, file uploads

The agent can be fast because it can't quietly skip these. I wrote more about why this matters in Code Got Cheap. Review Didn't.

When something breaks

/hb:debug has one rule I now follow without an agent too: no theory before a feedback loop.

Before reading code to guess a cause, the agent has to show one command that reproduces the bug. It must fail on the exact symptom, give the same result every run, and finish in seconds. A failing test, a curl, a headless browser script.

Only then does it list 3 to 5 ranked hypotheses, each with a prediction that could prove it wrong. That stops the agent from fixing the first plausible cause, which is the habit that wasted most of my debugging sessions.

flowchart TD
  accTitle: The debug loop
  accDescr: Build a feedback loop that fails, reproduce and minimize, list ranked hypotheses, test each one against the loop until it goes green, then fix and keep the loop as a regression test.
  loop[Failing loop] --> repro[Reproduce + minimize] --> hyp[3-5 ranked hypotheses]
  hyp --> test{Loop goes green?}
  test -- no, next hypothesis --> hyp
  test -- yes --> fix[Fix + regression test]

The flow improves itself

The last step is /hb:retro. It reads the session and suggests changes to the environment, not the code: a missing check, a rule in AGENTS.md that should be a lint rule, a file the agent took too long to find.

This is where moving off TracerKit pays off. A retro finding becomes a one-line edit in agent-skills, and every project picks it up on the next update.

Wrapping up

The spec is still at the center, as it was in v1. What changed is everything around it. The prompts I kept retyping are skills, and the reminders I kept giving are checks.

This flow will change again with the next tool or model. When it does, it will be a commit to agent-skills, and v4.

Related:

  • How I Use Claude Code to Build Features
  • Why I Built TracerKit
  • Skills Are the New CLI
  • Code Got Cheap. Review Didn't.

articles.title: Most Package Managers Won't Stop a Tampered Download by Default
articles.description: Trail of Bits tested 25 package managers against a compromised server. Only Go and vcpkg verified every download. Here's what to change in your CI.
articles.body_html:
Keegan Ryan of the security firm Trail of Bits set up a fake compromised package server and pointed 25 popular package managers at it. Two of them, Go and vcpkg, verified every package they downloaded, even without a lockfile. Without one, the other 23 installed whatever they were given.

Lockfiles didn't rescue most of them either.

The test

Ryan routed each tool's traffic through a proxy that could rewrite downloads, then installed quickstart projects with default settings, with and without a lockfile. An attack counted as a success if the injected code ran. The threat model assumes any web-facing server, such as a registry or a mirror, can be compromised, but backend secrets like private signing keys can't.

The lockfile is the safety net, and it's mostly unplugged

A lockfile pins every dependency's exact version and, ideally, a hash: a fingerprint the download has to match. Fewer than half of the 25 tools checked those hashes by default.

All 25 package managers, by default behavior. Source: Trail of Bits, October 14, 2026.

Nine verify when a lockfile is present, including npm, pnpm, Cargo, uv and Yarn. Five can verify, but only with extra steps. The last nine don't verify lockfile hashes at all, or the check doesn't apply to them.

Checks that don't stop anything

Tools with no check are the obvious failures. The sneakier ones run a check and install anyway:

  • Pub (Dart and Flutter) detects a hash mismatch, installs the package anyway and updates the lockfile to match, unless you pass --enforce-lockfile. Some Flutter commands run pub get too, and can overwrite the lockfile unless called with --no-pub.
  • pnpm overwrote the lockfile on a mismatch until version 11.4, in May 2026, so the tampered package simply became the new truth.
  • Composer (PHP) locks a Git commit, then downloads a ZIP archive it never checks against that commit.
  • CocoaPods hashes the package spec but fetches the source by Git tag, which a compromised host could serve with different contents.
  • cpanminus (Perl) still connects to its repository over plain HTTP by default.

Four outcomes when the download and the lockfile disagree. Only the green one protects you.

Why the defaults are like this

None of this is hidden; it's documented behavior. Lockfiles were built for reproducible installs, and as Ryan notes, reading them through a supply-chain lens "is a recent interpretation that can be at odds with their original design." Strict pinning also has a cost: every update, security fixes included, needs a lockfile change.

Go shows the alternative. It checks every hash against a signed checksum database that works like a transparency log, which makes targeted tampering much harder, at the cost of concentrating trust in a single private key. It was the only tool that verified every download and checked signatures by default. As Ryan puts it, "Package signing is in a similar state now to where HTTPS was a decade ago."

What to do this week

  1. Commit your lockfile, at least for applications. Norms for libraries vary by ecosystem.
  2. Install in strict mode in CI: npm ci, pnpm install --frozen-lockfile, uv sync --locked, pip install --require-hashes -r requirements.txt (with hashes generated by pip-compile --generate-hashes) or dart pub get --enforce-lockfile.
  3. If your tool needs extra steps, take them: the conda-lock library for Conda, a verification-metadata.xml file for Gradle, the RestorePackagesWithLockFile property for NuGet.
  4. If your tool is in the last group, don't treat its lockfile as a security control. Maven can check signatures against trusted keys with the third-party pgpverify-maven-plugin. Beyond that, the fallback Conan's developers suggest applies widely: if integrity is critical, run your own repository server.

Then test it: change one hash in your lockfile on purpose and confirm CI fails.

Caveats

Each tool was tested with one package, one version and one platform, Ubuntu, and some setups, like PowerShell and CocoaPods on Ubuntu, don't reflect typical use. The study shows that reasonable defaults can leave you exposed, not that every setup is.

Verification comes before detection

Most supply chain tooling hunts for packages already known to be bad. This study is about the step before that: making sure the package you got is the package you asked for. For most of the 25 tools, that check is off by default or missing. Where it exists, turning it on is about the cheapest security win you'll find.

If you check what your package manager does on a hash mismatch, I'd like to hear what you find.

Sources

  • Package managers have an integrity problem, Keegan Ryan, Trail of Bits, October 14, 2026

articles.title: I Built an AI That Remembers the Promises We Forget
articles.description: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady          ...
articles.body_html:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady

What I Built

The report was supposed to arrive yesterday. Somewhere in last week's notes, someone said they would send it. Before asking for an update, a researcher has to reconstruct the conversation: who offered, what they offered, and whether there was actually a deadline.

That is the fictional situation in my explicitly synthetic demo. It captures a familiar kind of work: remembering the small agreements that never became formal tasks.

I built PromiseKeeper to turn those agreements into a queue a person can check. Import meeting notes, a chat transcript, or a text file. A local language model proposes commitments. Every suggestion stays beside the exact words that support it. The reviewer can approve it, correct it, dismiss it, or mark it complete.

An approved promise can then become a polite follow-up draft. The person reviews and edits the wording, and decides whether to send it. PromiseKeeper has no sending integration.

The app is built around the difference between a possible promise and a confirmed one. “I'll send the report” deserves attention. “I already sent the report” describes something finished. “If the samples clear, I'll upload the appendix” carries a condition that should stay attached. An uncertain date should remain uncertain.

The interface gives those distinctions room: an evidence review inbox, upcoming and overdue summaries, a timeline, follow-up drafts, and local privacy controls. It supports pasted text and .txt or .md files. SQLite stores the sources and review decisions on the same machine as the local model.

The desired payoff is modest and concrete: bring the relevant promise back into view, with enough context to decide the next step.

I designed the workspace around reading and deciding: a left sidebar, vertically arranged input fields, and charcoal, forest-green and mint surfaces. Source quotes stay readable inside each card. The mobile drawer supports keyboard focus and Escape, and the help dialog explains the review boundary. Follow-up drafts can be copied or downloaded; source deletion lets the person check exactly what they are removing.

Demo

Watch the demo on YouTube. The redesigned interface is demonstrated in a 112.36-second, 1920x1080 recording narrated by genuine Kokoro-82M using af_sarah. The local export is saved at demo/assets/video/final_demo.mp4.

The recording follows a researcher importing five snippets of synthetic notes. Actual local Qwen inference finds three candidates: a revised field report, cleaned survey figures, and a conditional appendix. The already-delivered consent forms and vague conference thought stay out of the action queue.

The reviewer checks the quotes, approves the report, and sees one confirmed promise past its date. Two suggestions remain available for review.

The final action is preparing an editable follow-up. The draft asks whether the recorded timing has shifted; it does not assume the person has failed to deliver.

These are screenshots of the working application. The video preserves the browser's original action timing, with added scene holds for narration. Its edited runtime is not a processing benchmark.

Code

Browse PromiseKeeper on GitHub. The repository includes the frontend, backend, synthetic evaluation corpus, API tests, browser smoke test, real application screenshots, and recording and narration scripts. The recording and narration scripts reproduce the demo; generated video and WAV files are local outputs.

The code is MIT licensed. The selected Qwen model and Kokoro weights have their own licenses and are downloaded separately.

The manual setup uses Python 3.12+, Node 22+, and Ollama. Pull qwen3:8b, start the FastAPI service on port 9000, and run the Next.js frontend. The README contains the commands and a Docker Compose option. There is no paid inference service to configure.

Useful places to begin reading are backend/app/main.py for the extraction and review boundary, app/page.tsx for the user journey, and backend/eval/run_evaluation.py for the measured synthetic evaluation. demo/record_demo.ts and demo/narrate_demo.py reproduce the screen recording and voiceover.

How I Built It

The frontend uses Next.js and TypeScript. FastAPI handles import, local inference, validation, review updates, drafting, export and source deletion. SQLAlchemy stores the relationships in SQLite.

The processing path is small enough to inspect:

Notes → source document and paragraph fragments
      → local Ollama / Qwen extraction
      → schema validation and source-quote check
      → evidence-linked suggestions in SQLite
      → human review → approved promise → editable draft

The configured extractor is Qwen3 8B through Ollama. The locally inspected model reports 8.2 billion parameters and Q4_K_M quantization. The evaluation records the model digest, rather than relying only on a tag that could later point to different weights. Structured extraction runs at temperature zero with reasoning disabled.

The model proposes an action, owner, recipient, deadline, condition, certainty, evidence quote and next step. Pydantic checks the shape of those values. The API then independently verifies that each evidence quote is a literal substring of the original source text. A plausible quote that does not occur in the notes is rejected.

That boundary is useful, but deliberately limited. A quote can be present and still fail to support the proposed owner or claim. The source check establishes provenance; the reviewer still has to establish meaning. The interface keeps the quote beside the action so that check can happen where the decision is made.

The backend also applies conservative lexical rejection to obvious refusals, completed actions and hypothetical statements. An earlier development run exposed false positives in these cases. The final measurements therefore describe the combined prompt, model, schema checks and filters. They are not a score for the base model alone.

Dates need a similar distinction. Explicit dates can be stored directly. Relative timing can be interpreted only when a source timestamp is known. Without that anchor, the date stays unresolved. A missing owner is allowed to remain missing too; filling a field with a confident guess would make the queue less trustworthy.

Each source is split into paragraph fragments with character offsets. Evidence records preserve quotes and their locations. When the same extraction key repeats within an import, the API groups it while retaining distinct supporting quotes. This is normalized exact grouping, not semantic deduplication. Two differently phrased obligations can remain separate, and exact grouping has its own limits when conditions differ. Broader similarity matching needs more work before it should alter a person's action queue.

Review changes create audit events. A source deletion removes its linked commitments and drafts. The dashboard counts confirmed overdue items, and CSV export includes approved commitments with their evidence. The prototype is intended for a person's local machine; shared hosting, account permissions and encrypted storage are separate deployment concerns.

Follow-up drafting uses a deterministic template assembled from approved fields. It does not ask a second model to invent background context, recipients, or excuses. The local model's core job is finding candidate obligations in unstructured conversation. Once the person approves the fields, predictable drafting keeps the next step inspectable.

I checked the implementation with four backend API tests and a production build including TypeScript checks. The browser journey uses genuine local Qwen inference and covers file loading, quote inspection, owner/date/note edits, approval, editable draft copy and download, the timeline, CSV export, completion, source deletion and cancellation, help, mobile keyboard navigation and dark mode. A later import is checked to ensure it does not inherit the previous source timestamp. Automated axe checks report zero violations for the selected rules across 16 light/dark page, dialog and mobile-drawer states; that is a scoped automated check, not a complete manual accessibility audit. The recording runs the actual browser, backend and local model.

For extraction, I authored 55 labelled synthetic cases across 11 categories. The preserved run produced these results:

Check Measured result
Case-level commitment classification 40 true positives, 0 false positives, 0 false negatives
Owner exact match 30 of 35 eligible cases
Explicit calendar-date exact match 5 of 5 eligible cases
Accepted quote substring check 41 of 41 accepted candidate quotes

The owner result is the most useful warning in that table: the system can identify a possible obligation and still attribute it incorrectly. In this corpus, implicit-owner examples account for the five owner mismatches.

The perfect classification result is a small development-set observation. These cases are authored, repetitive, and were used while improving the pipeline. Quote validity is also an enforced acceptance rule, so its perfect rate is not independent evidence of understanding. The evaluation does not score claim entailment and does not cover sarcasm, multilingual conversations, noisy transcription, contradictions, or the full range of date language. The five date examples are a narrow check.

The corpus, evaluator and per-case outputs are preserved so a reader can inspect those limits and add harder examples. Real conversations and a held-out evaluation would be the next useful evidence.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

A commitment assistant handles information that can be mundane in isolation and sensitive in combination: who is waiting for whom, which deadline is slipping, and what people agreed to in a private discussion.

Running an open-weight extractor locally makes the data path understandable. After the model has been downloaded, inference does not need a hosted model account. The notes go from the local app to the configured local Ollama service, and the resulting records stay in SQLite. The demo uses synthetic material, but the architecture is chosen for conversations a person would want to keep private.

Open components also make failure inspectable. I can retain a failing synthetic example, adjust the prompt or acceptance filter, and run the same evaluator again. A model digest, a source quote, and a saved result give someone else something concrete to investigate. They can replace the model adapter and keep the validation and human review boundaries.

There are costs to that choice. An eight-billion-parameter model needs a substantial download and enough memory. Local inference can be slow or unavailable on a particular computer. Initial setup is more work than entering a hosted API key. The UI exposes model availability and processing failures because those constraints affect the user's experience.

The same approach carries into the video. Kokoro runs locally, its selected voice and weight hashes are recorded, and the narration script and caption timings are included. The demonstration can be regenerated from the project instead of depending on an unexplained media asset.

The Lazy Payoff

The visible transformation is five raw snippets becoming three candidate obligations, then one approved overdue report and an editable follow-up. The person makes the important decisions while the app gathers the relevant words into one place.

I have not measured saved hours, fewer missed deadlines, or reduced stress. The synthetic demonstration shows a workflow, and the evaluation measures a narrow extraction task. Neither establishes a productivity improvement for real teams.

The burden I want to reduce is repeatedly reconstructing the same agreement before taking a small, reasonable next step. Sometimes that step is sending a reminder. Sometimes it is noticing a condition and waiting. Sometimes it is rejecting the suggestion because there never was a promise.

Keeping that choice with the person matters as much as finding the sentence. A useful assistant should help us remember what we owe one another, while leaving room for people to explain what changed.

Prize Categories

Overall Slow and Steady challenge entry.

articles.title: Your AI Agent Says “Done.” What Did It Actually Verify?
articles.description: “Fixed the bug. All tests pass.”  Great.  Which tests? Did they run? Did they cover the bug—or did...
articles.body_html:
“Fixed the bug. All tests pass.”

Great.

Which tests? Did they run? Did they cover the bug—or did the agent change the test until it passed?

A confident completion message is easy to read as proof. But before you merge the changes, you need to understand what actually happened.

Here’s a simple workflow for checking an AI agent’s work without manually repeating every step.

1. Define “done” before it starts

“Fix the checkout bug” leaves too much open to interpretation.

Give the agent an observable outcome:

When a discount exceeds the order subtotal, the total should be zero. Add a regression test. Preserve valid discount behavior.

Now you have something concrete to verify.

For a UI task, describe the interaction. For an API task, specify the response and side effects.

Clear acceptance criteria make both implementation and verification easier.

2. Ask for evidence in the completion report

A useful report should include:

  • What changed.
  • Which commands ran.
  • Whether they passed or failed.
  • What could not be checked.

Compare these two reports:

“Everything works.”

And:

“Added a regression test for excessive discounts. The checkout test suite passed. Browser checkout was not tested because payment credentials were unavailable.”

The second report tells you what you can rely on and what still needs attention.

When your tool exposes execution logs, inspect them. A command mentioned in a summary is still a claim until you can confirm its execution.

3. Make sure the test catches the original bug

A passing test is useful only if it checks the behavior you care about.

Suppose the task is to prevent negative totals.

This assertion tells you almost nothing:

expect(result).toBeDefined();

This one checks the requirement:

expect(calculateTotal(50, 80)).toBe(0);

Where practical, confirm that the regression test fails against the original implementation and passes after the fix.

Then check nearby behavior:

expect(calculateTotal(50, 20)).toBe(30);

The goal is to demonstrate that the bug was fixed while preserving expected behavior.

4. Read changes to the tests themselves

Sometimes the implementation needs to change. Sometimes an outdated test needs to change too.

But a green result deserves closer inspection if the agent also:

  • Skipped a failing test.
  • Removed an important assertion.
  • Replaced realistic behavior with a convenient mock.
  • Changed the expected result to match the implementation.
  • Disabled a check in configuration.

These changes can have valid reasons. Ask for the reason and compare it with the requirement.

“Tests pass” has limited meaning if the relevant checks were weakened.

5. Match verification to the change

Different changes need different evidence.

Change Useful verification
Calculation Expected values and boundary cases
API endpoint Status, response body, permissions, and stored changes
Database migration Apply it to representative data and check compatibility
UI interaction Run the interaction and inspect the resulting state
Background job Check retries, duplicate handling, and failure behavior

A successful build proves that the build completed. It doesn’t prove that checkout works.

A screenshot shows appearance. It doesn’t prove that the button saves anything.

Choose checks that exercise the promised behavior.

6. Look for fixes that moved the problem

A small bug can lead to a surprisingly large patch.

Before merging, ask:

  • Did the agent change unrelated files?
  • Did it introduce a dependency for a small task?
  • Did it suppress an error instead of handling it?
  • Did it remove validation to make the request succeed?
  • Did it change a shared function and miss its other callers?

Start with the diff summary, then inspect the affected paths.

A large change isn’t automatically wrong. It should have an explanation proportional to its scope.

7. Treat blocked verification as unfinished verification

Sometimes the agent cannot run a check.

The database is unavailable. A dependency cannot be installed. Browser access is missing.

That is useful information.

The report should say:

“Implemented the change, but integration tests could not run because the test database was unavailable.”

Avoid turning “could not test” into “probably works.”

Record the missing check and complete it in the appropriate environment before relying on the result.

A prompt you can reuse

Add this to your next coding task:

Before editing, state the expected behavior and how you will verify it.

After editing, report:

  1. What changed.
  2. The exact checks you ran and their results.
  3. Whether the regression test catches the original failure, if applicable.
  4. Any tests or checks you changed, removed, or skipped—and why.
  5. What remains unverified.

Only claim a check passed if you actually ran it and observed a passing result.

This won’t eliminate mistakes. It gives you a clearer starting point for assessing the work.

Before you click merge

Ask one question:

“What evidence shows that this change meets the requirement?”

Sometimes the answer is a focused regression test. Sometimes it is an integration run, a browser interaction, or several checks together.

The important part is being able to connect the evidence to the task.

An AI agent can help you implement and verify a change. Its final message should make that verification inspectable.

What’s the biggest gap you’ve found between an agent saying “done” and the work actually being finished?

Today we celebrate the official release of version 2.0 of the MiniScript programming language!

Download MiniScript 2 here!

This is a complete rewrite, from the ground up, focused primarily on performance. The results do not disappoint: MiniScript 2 clocks in at 45X - 50X faster on some benchmarks, with an average of 10X - 15X faster across the board.

It also brings some cool language improvements, including:

  • Better error handling
  • Frozen lists and maps
  • Computed lists
  • Mark-and-sweep garbage collection, even in C++

Today's release includes a new & improved command-line build for Linux, Windows, Mac, and any .NET platform. This can be used interactively, with a powerful REPL (Read-Eval-Print Loop) that lets you reference earlier inputs and outputs; or it can be used to create scripts and programs to run from the command line. Those can include sophisticated terminal control, enabling interactive text user interfaces like this:

That's one of the examples included with the download; another one is a modern port of the classic "Super Star Trek" game:

But MiniScript 2 is not just for fun and games! The command-line environment includes full support for manipulating files and data, both text-based and binary; executing shell commands; reading the shell arguments; parsing JSON data; and more. Automate your workflows with a clean, modern scripting language that is a joy to read and write.

MiniScript 2.0 is the cornerstone of the 2026 MiniScript Road Map, and I'm delighted to say that it is shipping right on schedule. Meanwhile, we've made great progress in parallel on both raylib-miniscript and Mini Micro 2... so download MS2 now, and then stay tuned for more exciting news in the coming weeks!

articles.title: 616 Bytes to Add Up Sixteen Numbers
articles.description: A comma-separated line parsed with string.Split allocates ~616 bytes a call; the span-based Split that yields Range values allocates nothing. I measured both.
articles.body_html:
I was reading an allocation profile for a request handler that parses a line of comma-separated numbers off an upstream feed. The parse itself is three lines. Nothing in it says new. So I wasn't expecting the fat column of string and string[] allocations sitting right on top of it, climbing every second the feed stayed busy.

They were coming out of one method call: line.Split(',').

Where the bytes come from

Here's the parser, more or less how I'd written it and how I've written it a hundred times before:

static long ParseWithStringSplit(string line)
{
    long sum = 0;
    foreach (string field in line.Split(','))
        sum += int.Parse(field, CultureInfo.InvariantCulture);
    return sum;
}

Clean, correct, reads like a sentence. The problem is Split. For a line with sixteen fields it hands you back a string[] of length sixteen, and every one of those sixteen entries is a freshly allocated string holding one little number. That's an array plus sixteen substrings on the heap, used for a few microseconds, then dropped on the floor for the GC to sweep up. You call it once at startup and nobody cares. You call it a few thousand times a second and it's a steady drip into gen 0, and gen 0 collections aren't free.

The thing is, I didn't actually want those substrings. I never kept them. I parsed each one into an int and threw the string away. I was allocating sixteen strings purely to look at sixteen slices of a string I already had in my hand.

The span version never makes the substrings

Since .NET 8 there's a split that works directly over a ReadOnlySpan<char> and gives you back Range values instead of strings. You slice into the original span yourself, and int.Parse has taken a span since .NET Core 2.1, so nothing ever gets copied into a new string:

static long ParseWithSpanSplit(string line)
{
    long sum = 0;
    ReadOnlySpan<char> span = line;
    foreach (Range r in span.Split(','))
        sum += int.Parse(span[r], CultureInfo.InvariantCulture);
    return sum;
}

The logic is identical. The only difference is Range r instead of string field, and span[r] instead of the field. span[r] isn't a copy, it's a window onto the characters already sitting in line. No array, no substrings, nothing for the collector to chase.

I counted it

I don't trust my own intuition about allocations, so I wrote the smallest thing that would show the gap. Same sixteen-field line, both parsers, five million calls each. I read GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread() around each loop and took the best of seven rounds. Here's the output:

Both parsers sum the line to 7074. Good.

string.Split:  3,080,000,040 bytes,   1657.5 ms  (best of 7)
span Split  :             40 bytes,   1105.2 ms  (best of 7)

Allocated per call: string.Split 616 B, span 0 B
Time ratio (best of 7): span is 1.50x the throughput of string.Split

616 bytes a call to add up sixteen numbers. The span version: a flat 40 bytes for the whole five-million-call run, which rounds to zero per call. That 40 is a one-time constant, not something that scales with the work.

I ran it a few times and the allocation numbers didn't move a single byte, which is what I'd expect since they're structural. The timing wandered between about 1.5x and 1.7x the throughput depending on the round. I'm on a shared two-core container, not a quiet benchmark box, so I trust the allocation figure a lot more than the milliseconds. The honest read is: the span path is clearly faster here, and the real, repeatable win is that it stops allocating entirely.

When I don't bother

I'll say the obvious part out loud, because it's the part that matters more than the benchmark. If your parse runs once when the app boots, 616 bytes is nothing. Don't go rewriting readable code to save a few hundred bytes you allocate at startup and never again. string.Split is clearer, and clearer wins when the perf doesn't matter.

There are real limits to the span split too, and they bit me the first time I reached for it. It splits on every occurrence of the separator, full stop. There's no StringSplitOptions.RemoveEmptyEntries, no trimming, no cap on the number of pieces. If your input has empty fields you care about skipping, or you want the "split into at most 3" behaviour, you're either back on string.Split or writing that logic by hand. And because a span is a ref struct, this parser has to stay synchronous. You can't stash the span in a field or carry it across an await, so the moment your parsing wants to be async, this shape stops working.

So my rule is narrow on purpose. When the parse is sitting in a loop that runs often and I can see it in a profile, I switch to the span split and the allocations just disappear. Everywhere else I leave string.Split alone, because the only thing I'd be buying is a worse-looking method.

Here's the whole thing if you want to run it yourself. New console project targeting net10.0, drop this in Program.cs, dotnet run -c Release:

using System.Diagnostics;
using System.Globalization;

const string line = "1024,37,8,512,9,1,4096,16,64,2,128,256,7,3,900,11";

long expected = ParseWithStringSplit(line);
long actual = ParseWithSpanSplit(line);
if (expected != actual) { Console.Error.WriteLine("Parsers disagree"); return 1; }
Console.WriteLine($"Both parsers sum the line to {expected}. Good.\n");

const int iterations = 5_000_000;
const int rounds = 7;

var (splitBytes, splitMs) = Measure("string.Split", iterations, rounds, ParseWithStringSplit, line);
var (spanBytes, spanMs) = Measure("span Split  ", iterations, rounds, ParseWithSpanSplit, line);

Console.WriteLine($"\nAllocated per call: string.Split {splitBytes / (double)iterations:F0} B, span {spanBytes / (double)iterations:F0} B");
Console.WriteLine($"Time ratio (best of {rounds}): span is {splitMs / spanMs:F2}x the throughput of string.Split");
return 0;

static (long bytes, double ms) Measure(string name, int iterations, int rounds, Func<string, long> parse, string line)
{
    long bestBytes = long.MaxValue;
    double bestMs = double.MaxValue;
    for (int r = 0; r < rounds; r++)
    {
        long acc = 0;
        long before = GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread();
        var sw = Stopwatch.StartNew();
        for (int i = 0; i < iterations; i++) acc += parse(line);
        sw.Stop();
        long bytes = GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread() - before;
        if (acc == long.MinValue) Console.WriteLine(acc); // keep acc observable
        bestBytes = Math.Min(bestBytes, bytes);
        bestMs = Math.Min(bestMs, sw.Elapsed.TotalMilliseconds);
    }
    Console.WriteLine($"{name}: {bestBytes,14:N0} bytes, {bestMs,8:F1} ms  (best of {rounds})");
    return (bestBytes, bestMs);
}

static long ParseWithStringSplit(string line)
{
    long sum = 0;
    foreach (string field in line.Split(','))
        sum += int.Parse(field, CultureInfo.InvariantCulture);
    return sum;
}

static long ParseWithSpanSplit(string line)
{
    long sum = 0;
    ReadOnlySpan<char> span = line;
    foreach (Range r in span.Split(','))
        sum += int.Parse(span[r], CultureInfo.InvariantCulture);
    return sum;
}

Do you reach for the span split by default, or only after a profiler points at it? I'm curious where other people draw that line.

— still counting bytes nobody asked me to count
